papers.title_in_file: A Guide to Quantum Computing Benchmarking and Certification
papers.version_note: Web article by Chris Coleman, The Quantum Insider, August 12, 2022; page furniture and related-article text in the layer is garbled.
papers.what_it_is: A trade-press overview article on quantum computing benchmarking metrics (qubit counts, fidelity, connectivity, quantum volume, CLOPS, randomized and algorithmic benchmarking).

assertions.value: The author states that qubit number is a prominent comparison metric, but that comparing quantum systems is more about the balance between qubit quality and number.
assertions.anchor: Qubit number, logic vs physical qubits, p.2
quotes: Currently one of the most prominent comparison metrics quoted in literature is the qubit number.
So, it’s more about the balance between qubit quality and number when comparing quantum systems.

assertions.value: The author states that current QPUs lack rigorous error correction and that many physical qubits are encoded together to form a logical qubit, and that the number of physical qubits needed per logical qubit is related to physical qubit quality.
assertions.anchor: Qubit number, logic vs physical qubits, p.2
quotes: As the current generation of QPUs still lack rigorous error correction, they are noisy and lead to higher than ideal error rates.
the number of physical qubits needed to produce a single logical qubit is ultimately related to the quality of the physical qubits

assertions.value: The author defines the relaxation time T1 as the time for a qubit to spontaneously evolve from an excited state to the ground state, and the coherence time T2 as the duration the qubit frequency is well defined.
assertions.anchor: Coherence times to gate operation ratio, p.2-3
quotes: The relaxation rate: defined by the time it takes the qubit to spontaneously evolve from an excited state to the ground state. Often called T1.
The coherence time is the duration the frequency of the qubit is well defined, called T2.
assertions.certainty_reason: The article defines T1 and T2 in the coherence section.

assertions.value: The author states that superconducting technologies generally have coherence times in microseconds, while trapped ions can have coherence times into seconds and sometimes minutes.
assertions.anchor: Coherence times to gate operation ratio, p.3
quotes: superconducting
technologies generally have coherence times in the microseconds (μs) whereas optical systems such as the trapped ions can have
significantly larger coherence times, into seconds and sometimes even minutes.
assertions.reader_inference: No source is cited for these ranges.

assertions.value: The author states that optical systems have longer pulse widths, so the ratio of coherence time to gate application time may not be more impressive than for superconducting or semiconducting systems with pulses in nanoseconds.
assertions.anchor: Coherence times to gate operation ratio, p.3
quotes: the pulse widths and are also longer, meaning that the ratio of qubit coherence to gate application times may not be more impressive than superconducting or semiconducting systems with pulses in nanoseconds (ns) time frame.

assertions.value: The author defines fidelity as the probability that a qubit will be in a certain known quantum state after a specific gate operation, and states that acceptable single qubit fidelities are in general above 99%.
assertions.anchor: Single Qubit and Gate Fidelity, p.4
quotes: Strictly speaking the fidelity, expressed as a percentage, is the probability that a qubit will be in a certain known quantum state after a specific gate operation.
In general, acceptable single qubit fidelities are above 99%.
assertions.reader_inference: The threshold is stated without a source or an error-correction context.

assertions.value: The author states that quantum circuit performance is typically determined by two qubit gate fidelities, because two qubits are the smallest number that can check entanglement.
assertions.anchor: Single Qubit and Gate Fidelity, p.4
quotes: Typically, quantum circuit performance is determined by two qubit gate fidelities.
We specifically look at two qubits because this is the smallest number of qubits that can be used to check entanglement.

assertions.value: The author calls characterization of entangling gate fidelities Clifford-gate benchmarking because it involves Clifford algebra.
assertions.anchor: Single Qubit and Gate Fidelity, p.4
quotes: We call this type of characterization Clifford-gate benchmarking as it involves Clifford algebra
assertions.reader_inference: Clifford-gate benchmarking is usually tied to randomized benchmarking over Clifford group elements; the article's description is loose.

assertions.value: The author states that solid state devices generally have two to three directly entangleable neighbors per qubit, that distant qubits need SWAP gates which increase circuit depth, and that trapped ion systems have all-to-all connectivity and need no additional SWAP gates.
quotes: this results in solid state technologies generally only having two to three direct neighbors which can be directly entangled.
this increases the circuit depth and overall resources required for the information processing, an obvious disadvantage.
These types of QPUs therefore have an all-to-all qubit connectivity and do not require any additional SWAP gates

assertions.value: The article's second figure caption states that the IonQ trapped ion system shown has 11 qubits with all-to-all connectivity, that the largest offering accessible through AWS Braket is an 80 qubit system, and that IBM holds the record for the largest superconducting QPU with 127 qubits at the time of writing.
quotes: the all-to-all connectivity of the 11-qubit trapped ion system by IonQ
the largest offering currently accessible through AWS bracket is an 80qubit system
IBM hold the record of largest superconducting QPU with 127 qubits.
assertions.reader_inference: Dated to August 2022; the figures are a snapshot.

assertions.value: The author states that IBM developed quantum volume in 2018 and defines it as the size of the largest square circuit, with depth equal to width, that can be successfully run on the processor.
quotes: IBM developed an alternative metric in 2018 for evaluating QPU performance: Quantum volume (QV).
The quantum volume is defined as the size of the largest square circuit that can be successfully run on the processor.
assertions.certainty_reason: The article states its definition of quantum volume in the Quantum Volume section.

assertions.value: The author states that QV is usually expressed as a single value that is empirically measured and not theoretically calculated, and that it considers qubit number, error rates, cross talk and connectivity.
quotes: The quantum volume considers a range of different QPU properties such as qubit number, error rates, cross talk and connectivity.
QV is usually expressed as a single value that is empirically measured and not theoretically calculated.

assertions.value: The author gives an example: a computer that executes a depth 5 circuit on 5 qubits but fails at depth 6 on 6 qubits has a quantum volume of 32, which the text layer prints as 25 after a flat exponent.
quotes: a quantum computer that can successfully execute a circuit with depth of 5 on 5 qubits but fails to execute a depth-6 circuit on 6 qubits, would have a quantum volume of 25 or 32.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints the exponent flat.

assertions.value: The author states that run success is assessed by the probability distribution of the circuit outcome, and that distributions with a small statistical deviation are considered successful.
quotes: distributions with a small statistical deviation are considered successful
assertions.reader_inference: The article does not state the heavy output threshold used by the original QV protocol.

assertions.value: The author states that IBM suggested expressing QV on a logarithmic scale, and that IonQ suggested a similar redefinition as the algorithmic qubit, which looks at square circuits composed of two qubit entangling gates.
quotes: Recently modifications to the QV concept have been suggested by IBM where the QV is expressed as a logarithmic scale of QV.
Similar redefinition has been suggested by IonQ, where the log of QV was used to Algorithmic qubit.

assertions.value: The author states that QV depends on depth and width, so it relates performance to topology, error rates and size, and is increasingly used as a performance gauge because a single value gives an idea of overall or average performance.
quotes: it inherently helps relate QPU performance to its topology/connectivity, error rates and overall size.
quantum volume is increasingly being used as a QPU performance gauge as it is more holistic

assertions.value: The author states that QV is somewhat controversial because some processors have an inherent hardware advantage, and reports that trapped ion QV is several orders of magnitude higher than solid-state counterparts despite slower operations.
assertions.anchor: Quantum Volume, p.7; Fig. 3 caption, p.8
quotes: QV can be somewhat controversial metric as some processors have an inherent advantage due to their underlying hardware.
their QV is reported to be several orders of magnitude higher than their solid-state counterparts.
assertions.reader_inference: Attributed to reports; no numbers are given in the body text.

assertions.value: The author states that CLOPS, Circuit Layer Operations Per Second, relies on the definition of QV and measures how many QV circuits a QPU can execute per unit of time, and incorporates the quantum-classical runtime interaction.
quotes: This runtime interaction has been incorporated into a benchmark metric called Circuit Layer Operations Per Second or CLOPS.
CLOPS relies on the definition of QV and gives a measure of how many QV circuits a QPU can execute per unit of time.
assertions.certainty_reason: The article states its definition of CLOPS in the CLOPS section.

assertions.value: The author states that component speeds may not indicate overall QPU speed because algorithms require multiple calls to a QPU with quantum-classical interfacing, so the runtime system becomes critical to high performance.
quotes: algorithms requiring multiple calls to a QPU
the runtime system that allows for efficient quantum-classical communication becomes a critical aspect of the information processing and essential to achieving high performance

assertions.value: The article's fourth figure caption, taken from an arXiv paper, states that QV and the emerging CLOPS metric can in tandem evaluate speed of information processing across the stack, from qubit errors and SPAM to classical-quantum interfacing bottlenecks.
quotes: there are now emerging metrics such as CLOPS that in tandem can evaluate the speed of information processing on these systems.
qubit errors, state preparation and measurements (SPAM), and to bottlenecks in the information workflow related to classical-quantum interfacing.

assertions.value: The author states that quantum state tomography becomes infeasible for even moderately sized circuits and that conducting it leads to SPAM errors, so alternative practices are essential for scaling on NISQ devices.
quotes: Firstly, it becomes infeasible to apply QST to even moderately sized circuits
the very act of conducting a state tomography experiment leads to State-preparation and measurement (SPAM) errors.
assertions.reader_inference: The claim that tomography itself causes SPAM errors is loosely worded; SPAM errors are normally a property of the device, which tomography must be robust against.

assertions.value: The author describes randomized benchmarking as measuring the exponential decay rate of fidelity as a function of random gate sequence length, with the decay rate presumed to estimate the average error probability per gate.
quotes: In such protocols one simply measures the exponential decay rate of the fidelity as a function of the length of a random sequence of gates.
The measured decay rate is presumed to give an estimate of the average error probability per gate.

assertions.value: The author states that randomized benchmarking is a very low-level practice focused on qubit performance and does not give much information on higher levels of abstraction in the information processing workflow, and that models of the decay remain an active research area.
quotes: it is a very low-level benchmarking practice, usually focused on the qubit’s performance.
it does not give much information on higher level of abstraction on the information processing workflow.

assertions.value: The author states that algorithmic and volumetric benchmarking evaluates specific algorithms instead of random gates, tracking performance as a function of increasing circuit depth and width, at a higher abstraction level than randomized techniques.
quotes: evaluates instead of random gates, the performance of specific algorithms
the performance is tracked as a function of increasing quantum circuit depth and width.
at a higher abstraction level compared to randomized techniques

assertions.value: The author states that application specific benchmarks have been explored, including VQE for chemistry simulations and QAE for Monte Carlo sampling, and that the volumetric approach is valuable for assessing scalability of NISQ algorithms.
quotes: including using VQE for benchmarking in chemistry simulations, through to QAE for monte Carlo sampling.
highly valuable for assessing scalability of NISQ algorithms
assertions.reader_inference: No references are given for these examples.

assertions.value: The author states that state-of-the-art NISQ devices at the time have between a few tens to just over one hundred qubits.
quotes: Currently state-of-the-art NISQ available are between a few tens to just over one hundred qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: The article states this as the scope of devices it discusses, as of August 2022.

assertions.value: The author describes transpilation as an optimization step that maps the virtual quantum circuit to one using native gates of the target QPU, with a theoretically identical outcome.
quotes: transpilation occurs, this is an optimization step that maps the virtual quantum circuit to one that is more native to the desired hardware.
transforms it into one that would have an (theoretically) identical outcome based on native gates available to a specific QPU.

assertions.value: The author describes a workflow of defining the circuit, sending it to the hardware provider with transpilation, running it, then either error mitigation or feedback control, or benchmarking against expected outcomes or other technologies.
quotes: Either a level of error mitigation or feedback control is used to further optimize the algorithm/workflow, or benchmarking is carried out to directly compare results with expected outcomes or other technologies.

assertions.value: The author states that research aims at concrete and agreed upon benchmarking methods similar to the classical top500 benchmarks, and that until a more universal performance gauge is developed benchmarking remains active.
quotes: developing concrete and agreed upon methods similar to those used in classical systems such as the top500 benchmarks.
Until a more universal performance gauge is developed, benchmarking remains a very active and exciting space to track.
assertions.certainty_reason: The conclusion states that no universal gauge yet exists.

assertions.value: The article states that it highlights topics typically featured in benchmarking research: hardware and qubit characterization, circuit and gate-level errors, and certifying performance through algorithm deployment, and refers readers to a more detailed report on request.
quotes: Here we highlight some of the topics typically featured in benchmarking research
For a more detailed assessment of Quantum Computing Benchmarking, including detailed diagrams please contact us
assertions.certainty_reason: The introduction states the article's scope.
assertions.reader_inference: A trade-press overview with no original experiments and few citations.
